unit: history / health-people (Unity College, AQA thematic study AA Britain: Health and the people)

findings.claim: Smallpox vaccination "made compulsory" in 1852 - a timeline entry, a key fact, a revision prompt, the factors list, the conclusion, a knowledge-check option and five mark schemes across lessons 6 and 7 all give 1852.
findings.truth: The Vaccination Act 1853 first made infant smallpox vaccination compulsory in England and Wales. The 1840 Act had made vaccination free and banned variolation; 1867 and 1871 tightened enforcement. No Act of 1852 exists.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Vaccination Act' (list of Acts; 1853 named as the first compulsory one)

findings.claim: Flashcards 4 and 5 both have the answer "1796" ("_____ Jenner tests his theory ..." and "_____ (weeks later) The crucial test ...").
findings.truth: Two cards in one deck may not share an answer - the validator rejects the unit. Both cards were also broken timeline fragments with the heading run into the body text.

findings.claim: The 1911 National Insurance Act gave "sickness pay (10 shillings per week for 26 weeks)".
findings.truth: It paid 10 shillings a week for the first 13 weeks and 5 shillings a week for the next 13 - 26 weeks in total, but at two different rates.

findings.claim: "In 1844, a public demonstration during a tooth extraction was considered a failure when the patient appeared to still feel pain."
findings.truth: Horace Wells had his own tooth pulled under nitrous oxide on 11 December 1844, which worked. The failed public demonstration at Massachusetts General Hospital was January 1845.

findings.claim: Two mark schemes date Pare running out of boiling oil to the siege of Turin in 1536.
findings.truth: Pare went to Italy with the French army for the Piemont campaign of 1537-38; the standard date is 1537, which is what lessons 11 and 14 of this same unit give.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Ambroise Pare' (Piemont campaign 1537-1538); internal consistency with L11 and L14

findings.claim: "Cholera arrived in Britain in 1831, killing over 50,000 people." Repeated on a flashcard.
findings.truth: The 50,000-plus death toll belongs to the 1848-49 epidemic, which killed about 52,000 in England and Wales. The 1831-32 epidemic killed far fewer. The figure has been reattached to 1848-49; no new figure was invented for 1831-32.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia '1846-1860 cholera pandemic' ("began in England and Wales in 1848, and claimed 52,000 lives")

findings.claim: Timeline entry "1884 - Koch identifies the cholera bacterium", placed between the 1861 and 1867 entries.
findings.truth: The rest of the unit dates it 1883 (lesson 8 twice, and two mark schemes in lesson 10 itself), and the entry broke the timeline's chronology. Re-dated 1883 and moved after the 1875 entry, so the run is 1842, 1848, 1854, 1858, 1861, 1867, 1875, 1883.
findings.evidence: internal consistency with L8 and L10's own mark schemes

findings.claim: "Andreas Vesalius was a Belgian anatomist."
findings.truth: Belgium was not founded until 1830. Vesalius was born in Brussels in 1514 in the Habsburg Netherlands and is normally described as Flemish.

findings.claim: Ibn al-Nafis "correctly argued that blood circulated around the body and passed through the lungs".
findings.truth: He described pulmonary circulation - blood passing through the lungs instead of through pores in the wall of the heart. Circulation round the whole body was Harvey's. The lesson's own timeline entry states it correctly, so the article contradicted itself.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Ibn al-Nafis'; internal contradiction with the lesson timeline

findings.claim: "By WWII, the first blood banks were set up."
findings.truth: Lesson 9 of this unit dates the first blood bank to 1917, for the Battle of Cambrai. The two lessons contradicted each other.

findings.claim: Lister "reduced the death rate from gangrene in his male surgical ward from 46% to 15% between 1864 and 1866".
findings.truth: 1864-66 is his period BEFORE antiseptics; his first antiseptic operation was August 1865, so the fall cannot have happened inside that window. I could not reach a source for the exact after-period years, so the false window was removed rather than replaced with a new one.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with the lesson's own August 1865 date

findings.claim: The poverty line of "21 shillings per week (about GBP 1.08)".
findings.truth: Twenty shillings made a pound, so 21 shillings is GBP 1.05.

findings.claim: Two revision prompts show stray backslashes on screen: "why Par\'e\'s ligatures were better" and "the year of Rontgen\'s discovery".
findings.truth: Escape characters left in the text. Corrected to Pare's and Rontgen's with the proper accents.

findings.claim: "This evaluative thinking ... is what examiners reward at the highest levels."
findings.truth: No published source states what examiners reward in these terms, and the house rule forbids asserting a board's marking. Rewritten as what the strongest answers do.
findings.evidence: house rule on copyright distancing and invented examiner claims

findings.claim: Collapsible heading "Why is genetic medicine increasingly examined in GCSE History?"
findings.truth: The specified content for this option names the pharmaceutical industry, penicillin, new diseases and antibiotic resistance, alternative treatments, and 21st-century healthcare costs and choices. It does not name genetics, DNA or the Human Genome Project. The material is defensible under 'new diseases and treatments', but the claim about what is examined is not. Heading reworded.

findings.claim: Model answer: "prescription charges were introduced by 1951, and Bevan resigned in protest".
findings.truth: The 1951 budget introduced charges for dentures and spectacles, which is what the lesson body correctly says. The shilling prescription charge came in 1952.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with the lesson body

findings.claim: "Hunter argued that surgeons and barbers should be separated and that surgery should become a respected profession."
findings.truth: Surgeons broke away from the barbers in 1745 to form the Company of Surgeons, when Hunter was 17; the royal charter that made it the Royal College of Surgeons came in 1800, seven years after his death. His campaign was for status and science, not for the separation.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Royal College of Surgeons of England' (1745 break from the barbers; charter 1800)

findings.claim: Cards 4 and 5 of every deck except lessons 1 and 3 are machine-cut fragments: headings run into body text ("Key Fact In _____ average life expectancy ...", "_____ key publication and its impact In 1543, Vesalius published ..."), mangled possessives ("Vesaliuss", "Londons", "Kings"), a sentence cut off mid-figure ("grew from about 1 million people in 1801 to over 5"), answers sitting inside their own question ("Louis", "Paul", "Healthcare"), and prompts asking for a filler word ("Instead", "Factor").
findings.truth: 26 cards across 13 lessons. All rewritten as What/Which/Who/When questions with a single clean answer, keeping every answer unique in its deck.

findings.claim: Eleven definition-front cards contain their own answer, for example "Measures taken to protect public health ..." answered "public health", "Hospitals funded by charitable donations and voluntary contributions ..." answered "voluntary hospitals", and "The practice of preventing infection during surgery" answered "antiseptic surgery".
findings.truth: Reshaped as 'Which term means ...?' questions that no longer give the answer away.

findings.claim: "Nightingale's reforms at Scutari cut the death rate from 42% to just 2%" - in a key fact, the timeline, a knowledge check and a model answer in lesson 13.
findings.truth: The figures are real for February to June 1855, but the fall followed the Sanitary Commission's flushing of the sewers under the hospital in March 1855, so crediting it to her ward reforms is contested. Option (a): leave it as the taught narrative. Option (b): keep the figures and add that the Sanitary Commission cleared the drains, which keeps the knowledge-check answer intact and is what a top-band answer needs. I recommend (b), and it should be decided once for this unit and its free-tier twin, where the same claim was raised.
findings.evidence: standard historiography of Scutari; same item raised as ADJUDICATE in history-aqa__britain-health-people

findings.claim: "Even Winston Churchill spoke out against the plans, calling the NHS 'a curse on the country.'"
findings.truth: I could not find this quotation in any source I could reach, and a quotation put in a named politician's mouth must be real. What is documented is that the Conservative Party opposed the NHS Bill. The quotation was removed and replaced with that fact; no new words were put in Churchill's mouth.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Aneurin Bevan' ("overcame political opposition from both the Conservative Party and from within his own party"); no source found for the quoted phrase

findings.claim: Galen's dominance is "over 1,500 years" in lesson 1 and in lesson 1's knowledge-check answer, but "over 1,300 years" in lesson 5's glossary, flashcard and dfn, and in a lesson 6 model answer.
findings.truth: Both statements are true, so neither is an error, but a student who reads lesson 5 and then meets lesson 1's knowledge check sees a different number. Left alone; worth aligning on 1,500 if the decks are ever regenerated.

findings.claim: Lister's antiseptic surgery is dated 1867 in lessons 3 and 8 but 1865 in lesson 9.
findings.truth: Both are right - first use on James Greenlees in August 1865, Lancet paper in 1867 - and lesson 9 explains both. No edit needed.

findings.claim: The matching check asks students to place Abulcasis as the 'Father of Modern Surgery', but Abulcasis is taught in lesson 3, not lesson 2.
findings.truth: The fact is right; the check simply tests content the lesson has not covered yet.

findings.claim: "Manchester grew from 334,000 to over 2.1 million."
findings.truth: Those are Greater Manchester's figures (328,609 in 1801; 2,357,150 in 1901), not the city's - the city of Manchester peaked at 766,311 in 1931. Broadly right but loosely labelled; not corrected because the numbers do match the wider area.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Demography of Greater Manchester'; 'History of Manchester' (1931 peak 766,311)

findings.claim: "After Rome fell in 410 AD, much knowledge was lost" (lesson 1, and repeated in a lesson 2 model answer).
findings.truth: 410 is the sack of Rome by Alaric and the year the legions left Britain. The fall of the Western Empire is conventionally dated 476. Reworded to 'sacked in 410 AD and the Western Empire collapsed'.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Fall of the Western Roman Empire' (476 the conventional marker; 410 the sack)

findings.claim: Duplicate glossary entries: 'laudable pus' twice in lesson 3, 'Yersinia pestis' twice in lesson 4, 'spontaneous generation' twice in lesson 8.
findings.truth: Harmless repetition rather than an error; not worth an edit.

findings.claim: No lesson in the unit sets a source-utility question, although that is one of the four question forms in this section of the paper.
findings.truth: The 90 questions that are set do match the paper: significance at 8 marks, two ways similar or different at 8 marks, and the factors essay at 16 plus 4 for spelling, punctuation and grammar. The gap is missing practice, not a wrong claim, so no edit was made.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2 Paper 2 Section A question table

findings.claim: Revision prompt: "name 3 reasons Fleming couldn't develop penicillin after his 1929 discovery".
findings.truth: Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 and published in 1929, as the lesson's own timeline says.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with the lesson timeline

findings.claim: A flashcard answer runs to 32 words, over the 30-word limit.
findings.truth: Shortened to 26 words with the same meaning.

findings.claim: Thirty-four further flashcards put a bare definition on the front with no question mark - the generator's glossary-card shape - instead of asking 'Which word or term means ...?'
findings.truth: The eleven that gave their own answer away were fixed here (F19). The rest are not wrong, only off-pattern, and the same shape appears in every deck this generator built, so fixing 34 cards in this one unit would leave the rest of the fleet inconsistent. Options: (a) convert these 34 now; (b) leave them and run one pipeline-level sweep across every unit. I recommend (b).

findings.claim: Fourteen of the fifteen lesson descriptions run over the 100-character limit (111 to 137 characters; lesson 4 is exactly 100).
findings.truth: Not a factual fault and shortening all fourteen is style work rather than fact-checking, so no edits were made. Worth a pass if the browse cards truncate.

summary: Fifteen lessons checked against the spec and against Wikipedia, with the free-tier twin's report used as a cross-check. The exam furniture is sound: every practice question is one of the three written forms this section sets, at the right marks (significance 8, two ways similar or different 8, factors essay 16 plus 4 for spelling, punctuation and grammar), no board is named anywhere in student-facing text, and no banned band label appears. The substance was mostly right, but eighteen factual or exam claims were wrong: compulsory vaccination dated 1852 instead of 1853 in twelve places including a knowledge-check option, the 1911 sick-pay rates, Wells's failed demonstration dated 1844, Pare's siege dated 1536 against 1537 elsewhere in the unit, the 1848-49 cholera death toll attached to 1831, Koch's cholera bacterium dated 1884 and out of sequence, Vesalius called Belgian, Ibn al-Nafis credited with full circulation, blood banks dated to WWII against 1917 in lesson 9, Lister's figures dated to a window that ends before his first antiseptic operation, a Churchill quotation no source supports, and an invented claim about what examiners reward. Alongside those, 37 flashcards were repaired: two cards in lesson 7 shared an answer, which fails the validator, and 26 cards across 13 lessons were machine-cut fragments with headings run into body text, mangled possessives and answers sitting inside their own question. 85 edits, two ADJUDICATE items and seven NOTEs.
